fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Accumulation, Ayurveda and Society as One Body", "body": "Chance frames Ryan Kemp's book The Age of Separation as an Ayurvedic reading of accumulation applied to society as one larger organism, where ideas and identifications can build up and cause disease much as material accumulation does. Ryan says Ayurveda names the first stage of disease sanchaya, and that studying it in Kerala showed him where Ayurveda and yoga intertwine. His argument is that whatever a person takes in, from beliefs to knowledge, needs a matching output free of righteousness, or it leads to disequilibrium. Chance suggests breath and movement practices build a healthy pranic accumulation, while Ryan replies that prana flows through the chakras rather than stacking up."}, {"title": "Calcified Belief and the Hunger for Identity", "body": "Ryan describes belief as information that should stay fluid, and says that once it calcifies into a collective identity it breeds judgment and violence, a point he credits to Krishnamurti. Chance reads passages from the book on consuming ideologies and fandoms, and both men tie that habit to shrinking attention, with Chance admitting the tug of his phone at a red light. Ryan answers with the self-inquiry of Ramana Maharshi, asking who you are without your phone and your digital identity, and with the Vipassana view that no one of the body's changing particles is the I."}, {"title": "Priceless, Not Worthless: Beyond Transactionality", "body": "The conversation treats transactionality as the illusion that every exchange must be equal in value. Chance points to indigenous customs where returning an equivalent gift reads as a rejection, and prefers the word permeable to vulnerable because a permeable person lets feelings pass through. He argues that unpaid labor and a few conscious breaths are priceless rather than worthless, and that close relationships need no scorecard. Ryan adds that a gift is not a gift while you cling to reciprocity, that we expect gifts in a certain form, and that hardship can arrive as one, citing Ram Dass on suffering as grace."}, {"title": "Babylon, Confusion and the Middle Way", "body": "Chance and Ryan agree that craving the marketplace and fleeing it both keep a person tethered to it, and that the middle way is to use the value system without getting caught in it. Ryan says an Aramaic scholar told him the name Babylon comes from a word meaning to confuse, and points to cobalt mined for computers as a sign that every choice steps on someone. Chance links Babylon to the Tower of Babel and argues that Latin and legalese work as calcified control languages. Both then contrast co-destruction with co-creation, with Ryan citing Charles Eisenstein."}, {"title": "Pedestals, Personas and Nonverbal Liturgy", "body": "Chance argues that neither oneself nor a teacher belongs on a pedestal, since that arrangement is where separation enters, and he observes that the appearance of knowledge gets monetized through the right look and follower counts. Ryan replies that trendy concepts invite a superficial first pass, which still counts as part of the path, and that spirituality is a demolition project rather than a tally of credentials, so the less a person clings to, the more power and worth he says they hold. Chance allows that outfits can signal without becoming identity, and Ryan likens clothing to liturgy, a nonverbal invitation toward harmony rather than manipulation."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Ryan Kemp is the author of The Age of Separation, a text that combines aspects of Buddhism, yogic philosophy, Ayurveda, indigenous wisdom, psychedelic experiences and more. In this conversation we discuss ideas from his book with the InnerVerse perspective.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Ego Is Not the Enemy", "body": "Chance opens the extension questioning whether ego can or should be eliminated from the self, suggesting that suffering and desire feed growth and that adults are simply good at pretending they are not pretending. Ryan answers that ego is not bad but a structure for handling endless stimuli, and asks which part of the ego would be left to do the killing. He separates ego from self, saying the two of us is the ego and the one of us is the self, and treats meditation as dropping into the witness."}, {"title": "Shells, Sheaths and Growing Past Limits", "body": "Ryan retells a rabbi's lobster story, where the animal must leave its shell and be exposed before growing a larger one, and pairs it with Ram Dass calling death the removal of a tight-fitting shoe. Chance extends the image to a hermit crab, saying the shell is built from the surrounding land, so there is never real separation, only identification with one shell and then another. Ryan then walks through the five sheaths of yoga, from body to breath, mind and wisdom to the self, framing ego as who you think you are and self as who you are."}, {"title": "Nothingness That Proves Existence", "body": "Chance argues that nothingness describes the eternal process of becoming rather than non-existence, using a squirrel with no name to contrast nature with a system that needs a full name and a birth date to identify you. He adds that the very concept of no thing proves existence. Ryan links this to the Heart Sutra, saying God cannot be captured in language because language freezes a process, and to Nassim Haramein on the vacuum behind empty space. He also reads Buddhist non-self and yogic Self as the same place, the non-clinging self."}, {"title": "Dependent Origination and the Original Moment", "body": "Ryan explains dependent origination, the Buddhist idea that things exist only because other things exist, and says it dissolves claims of originality and, in his view, regret, since no moment could have gone differently. Chance flips it, arguing every moment is original because each emerges from timelessness. Ryan then describes the innocence he learned in Ashtanga yoga, open and trusting without being naive, and Chance cautions that innocence can shade into ignorance, so that we must consciously manage our own fear."}, {"title": "Love, Boundaries and Healing Through Change", "body": "Ryan says people flee discomfort and that unloved emotions resurface like whack-a-mole, while loving them lets the defenses guarding the heart release. Chance sets love as recognition of every potential against fear as control, then tells the scorpion and frog parable to argue for honesty with oneself and for choosing boundaries consciously. Ryan calls boundaries the masculine structure that lets the feminine vine bloom, admits he traveled long without any, and closes on his belief that changing yourself changes the world around you."}]

fields.Plus Quotes JSON: [{"text": "The difference between adults and children is that adults are so good at pretending that they're not pretending that they forgot that they're pretending.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "What part of the ego is gonna kill the ego? It's an interesting thing to play a zero-sum game battle with yourself.", "author": "Ryan Kemp", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/9ebd8af7-5ef5-467a-950a-eb6bb36d8383/RYAN-KEMP.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "The ego is who you think that you are, and the self is who you are.", "author": "Ryan Kemp", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/9ebd8af7-5ef5-467a-950a-eb6bb36d8383/RYAN-KEMP.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "If you see a squirrel, he's just what he is. He's a process that's part of the land, he doesn't have a name like Kevin or something.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "You can't separate any specific moment in your life and think that that shouldn't have happened.", "author": "Ryan Kemp", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/9ebd8af7-5ef5-467a-950a-eb6bb36d8383/RYAN-KEMP.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "Every moment is original, as in the origin is source and eternity, and every moment is emerging out of timelessness.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "The more that we're able to love our wounds, the more that we see that the wound is guarding the heart.", "author": "Ryan Kemp", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/9ebd8af7-5ef5-467a-950a-eb6bb36d8383/RYAN-KEMP.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "Love's answer is love no matter what. So it allows for all these various expressions, and then love is still there.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "Loving ourselves is also being honest and not lying to ourselves, even about whether or not somebody is a scorpion that might sting us and cause us to both drown.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "We have to allow ourselves to continually navigate our own crevices and cracks until the light is just pouring in.", "author": "Ryan Kemp", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/9ebd8af7-5ef5-467a-950a-eb6bb36d8383/RYAN-KEMP.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}]
fields.Quotes JSON: [{"text": "The more that we get caught in the quantifiable realm, the less we can actually dip into the qualitative aspects of life.", "author": "Ryan Kemp", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/9ebd8af7-5ef5-467a-950a-eb6bb36d8383/RYAN-KEMP.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "The funny thing about being is you're already doing. Being is a verb right there.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "I think that presence is emptiness. And I think that gratitude is emptiness because within that emptiness you're being filled.", "author": "Ryan Kemp", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/9ebd8af7-5ef5-467a-950a-eb6bb36d8383/RYAN-KEMP.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "If you're vulnerable, then you can be hurt. But we also can't put someone that we're looking at as a teacher on a pedestal.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "Spirituality is a deconstruction process, it's a demolition project.", "author": "Ryan Kemp", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/9ebd8af7-5ef5-467a-950a-eb6bb36d8383/RYAN-KEMP.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "Nothingness is important because it's the power to forget also.
